question:
Identify the error in the tense of the sentence and select the option that correctly rectifies the error.
Between two evils, I always picks the one I have never tried before.
option_1: Between two evils, I always pick the one I have never tried before.
option_2: Between two evils, I always is picking the one I have never tried before.
option_3: Between two evils, I always picked the one I have never tried before.
option_4: Between two evils, I always picking the one I have never tried before.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Between two evils, I always pick the one I have never tried before.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence describes a habitual action (something the speaker always does), which must be expressed in the Simple Present Tense.

• Rule — Subject-Verb Agreement in Simple Present Tense: With the subject "I", the verb must be in its base form (V1), not the -s/-es form. The -s/-es form of the verb is used only with third person singular subjects (he, she, it, or a singular noun).

• The original sentence wrongly uses "picks" (the third-person singular form) with the first-person subject "I". It must be corrected to the base form "pick".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is incorrect because "is picking" is the Present Continuous Tense, which is used for an action happening right now, not for a habitual/general truth.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "picked" is the Simple Past Tense, which does not fit the timeless, habitual sense of the sentence (indicated by "always").

• Option 4 is incorrect because "picking" alone (without an auxiliary "is/am/are") is not a complete, grammatically correct verb form.

NOTE

• With the subjects I, we, you, they, and plural nouns, the verb takes its base form in the Simple Present Tense; with he, she, it, and singular nouns, an -s/-es is added.

• Adverbs of frequency like always, usually, often, never, sometimes are strong indicators of the Simple Present Tense in SSC error-spotting and tense questions.

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
The teacher will / certainly help you / if you will / ask her.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. if you will.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence is a Conditional Sentence Type 1 (a first conditional, used for real/possible future situations): "The teacher will certainly help you if you ask her."

• Rule — Conditional Sentence Type 1: If + Subject + Simple Present Tense, Subject + will/shall + base verb (V1). The if-clause (the condition) must always be in the Simple Present Tense; the auxiliary "will" is never used in the if-clause itself.

• In the given sentence, the if-clause "if you will ask her" wrongly uses "will". It must be corrected to the Simple Present: "if you ask her."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "certainly help you" is correct as it is; it forms part of the main/result clause "The teacher will certainly help you", which correctly uses will + base verb.

• Option 2: "The teacher will" is correct as it is; it is the subject and auxiliary of the main clause, correctly followed by the base verb "help".

• Option 4: "ask her" is correct as it is; once "will" is removed from the if-clause, "ask her" is the correctly required base-verb form.

NOTE

• The if-clause of a Type 1 conditional never takes will, would, shall, or should — a very frequently tested SSC error.

• Compare with Conditional Type 2 (If + Past Simple, would + V1) and Conditional Type 3 (If + Past Perfect, would have + V3), which are used for unreal/hypothetical situations.

question:
The following sentence has been divided into three segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. If you don't find any error, select 'No error' as your answer.
It was possible to achieve anything, / if one has the grit and determination / to keep going.
option_2: It was possible to achieve anything,
option_3: if one has the grit and determination
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. It was possible to achieve anything,

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence describes a general truth/habitual fact (that grit and determination make anything achievable), which requires consistency of tense throughout, normally the Simple Present Tense.

• Rule — Tense Consistency: When one part of a sentence uses the Simple Present Tense (as seen in "if one has the grit and determination"), the other clauses referring to the same general truth must also use the Simple Present Tense, not the past tense.

• The segment "It was possible to achieve anything," wrongly uses the past tense "was". It should be corrected to the present tense: "It is possible to achieve anything,".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "No error" is incorrect because the sentence does contain a tense-consistency error, as explained above.

• Option 3: "if one has the grit and determination" is correct as it is; it correctly uses the Simple Present Tense "has", consistent with a general truth.

• Option 4: "to keep going." is correct as it is; the infinitive "to keep going" is grammatically appropriate and needs no change.

NOTE

• SSC error-spotting questions frequently test tense consistency — once a sentence establishes a tense for a general/habitual statement, every clause referring to that same idea must match it.

• Watch especially for a lone past-tense verb (like "was", "had", "did") sitting among otherwise present-tense clauses.

question:
The following sentence has been divided into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
My Vice-Chancellor works / eighteen hours / a day, / seven days week.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. seven days week.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence describes how often the subject works, using two parallel time expressions: "eighteen hours a day" and "seven days a week".

• Rule — Frequency/Time Expressions: Expressions like "a day", "a week", "a month", "a year" use the indefinite article "a" in the sense of "per" (e.g., "twice a day" = "twice per day"). The article cannot be dropped.

• The segment "seven days week." wrongly omits the article "a" before "week". It must be corrected to "seven days a week.", matching the parallel structure of "a day" earlier in the sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "My Vice-Chancellor works" is correct as it is; it is a grammatically sound subject + verb (Simple Present Tense, correctly agreeing with the singular subject).

• Option 3: "eighteen hours" is correct as it is; it is a straightforward noun phrase indicating duration.

• Option 4: "a day," is correct as it is; the article "a" is correctly used here in the sense of "per day".

NOTE

• Common SSC-tested phrases using "a/an" in the sense of "per": once a day, twice a week, three times a month, a dollar a dozen.

• Always check that parallel time expressions in a sentence (like "a day" and "a week" here) are structured consistently.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Organic agriculture offers a means to substitute costlier agricultural inputs such as HYV seeds, chemical fertilisers and pesticides with locally produced organic inputs that are cheaper and thereby generate good returns on ______1______. Organic agriculture also generates income through exports as the demand for organically grown crops is on a _____2___. Studies across countries have shown that organically grown food has more nutritional value than chemical farming, thus providing us with healthy foods. Since organic farming requires more labour input than ____3___ farming, India will find organic farming an attractive______4____. Finally, the produce is pesticide-free and produced in an environmentally ____5____ way.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. investment.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The passage states that organic inputs are cheaper than costly chemical inputs like HYV seeds, fertilisers and pesticides, and that using them **"generates good returns on ___". The standard collocation for money put into a venture yielding returns is "return on investment"**.

• Rule — Collocation-based Cloze Filling: In a cloze passage, the blank must be filled with the word that both fits the grammar of the sentence and forms the natural, idiomatic collocation used in standard English/economics writing. "Good returns on investment" is a fixed, commonly used phrase.

• Since the passage's central idea is substituting costly inputs with cheaper ones to earn more from the money spent (invested) in farming, "investment" is the only option that logically and idiomatically completes the sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "loss" is incorrect because it contradicts the positive meaning of "good returns" — one earns good returns ON an investment, not on a loss.

• Option 2: "profit" is incorrect because "returns on profit" is not idiomatic; profit is itself a type of return, not something returns are generated "on".

• Option 3: "expenditure" is incorrect because, while related in meaning, "returns on expenditure" is not the standard/idiomatic collocation used in economics texts — "return on investment" is the fixed phrase.

NOTE

• Common fixed economics/business collocations tested by SSC: return on investment, cost of production, rate of interest, source of income.

• In cloze passages, always read the whole surrounding sentence before choosing an option — the correct word is usually the one forming a standard collocation, not merely one that "sounds okay" in isolation.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Organic agriculture offers a means to substitute costlier agricultural inputs such as HYV seeds, chemical fertilisers and pesticides with locally produced organic inputs that are cheaper and thereby generate good returns on ______1______. Organic agriculture also generates income through exports as the demand for organically grown crops is on a _____2___. Studies across countries have shown that organically grown food has more nutritional value than chemical farming, thus providing us with healthy foods. Since organic farming requires more labour input than ____3___ farming, India will find organic farming an attractive______4____. Finally, the produce is pesticide-free and produced in an environmentally ____5____ way.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. rise.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence states that organic agriculture **"generates income through exports as the demand for organically grown crops is on a ___". Since exports generate income, the demand referred to must be increasing**, not decreasing or unchanging.

• Rule — Contextual Logic in Cloze Passages: The chosen word must agree with the cause-and-effect logic of the sentence — here, rising demand is the cause of increased export income.

• "On a rise" correctly conveys that demand is going up, which logically explains why organic agriculture is able to generate more income through exports.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "decline" is incorrect because a decline in demand would reduce export income, contradicting the sentence's positive statement about generating income.

• Option 3: "growth" is incorrect because, although related in meaning to increase, "on a growth" is not an idiomatic collocation with the preceding article "a" — English does not say "demand is on a growth".

• Option 4: "stagnation" is incorrect because stagnation means no change/growth, which would not help generate additional income through exports.

NOTE

• Common idiomatic phrases with "rise": on the rise, a sharp rise, to give rise to.

• Distinguish "rise" (increase, noun/verb) from "raise" (to lift or increase something, always a transitive verb) — a frequently tested pair in SSC vocabulary questions.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Organic agriculture offers a means to substitute costlier agricultural inputs such as HYV seeds, chemical fertilisers and pesticides with locally produced organic inputs that are cheaper and thereby generate good returns on ______1______. Organic agriculture also generates income through exports as the demand for organically grown crops is on a _____2___. Studies across countries have shown that organically grown food has more nutritional value than chemical farming, thus providing us with healthy foods. Since organic farming requires more labour input than ____3___ farming, India will find organic farming an attractive______4____. Finally, the produce is pesticide-free and produced in an environmentally ____5____ way.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. conventional.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence compares the labour requirement of organic farming with another type of farming: **"organic farming requires more labour input than ___ farming". The natural contrast to "organic farming" (which avoids chemical inputs) is "conventional farming"** (traditional, chemical-input-based farming).

• Rule — Contextual Contrast in Cloze Passages: The passage repeatedly contrasts organic farming with ordinary, chemically-assisted farming (referred to earlier as "chemical farming"). The missing word must refer to this same standard type of farming that organic farming is compared against.

• "Conventional farming" is the standard term used (in agriculture and economics writing) for farming that relies on chemical fertilisers and pesticides rather than organic methods, making it the most logical and commonly used term here.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "insipid" is incorrect because it means "dull/tasteless/lacking flavour" and does not describe a type of farming at all.

• Option 2: "mechanical" is incorrect because it refers to machine-based processes, not specifically to the chemical-input-based farming being contrasted with organic farming here.

• Option 3: "rigorous" is incorrect because it means "thorough/strict/demanding" and does not name a type of farming; it does not fit as a description of "farming" being contrasted with "organic".

NOTE

• "Conventional" means "based on what is traditionally done; standard, usual" — frequently used in exam passages to contrast with "organic", "modern", or "alternative" methods.

• Related word: "unconventional" (not conforming to what is normally done).

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Organic agriculture offers a means to substitute costlier agricultural inputs such as HYV seeds, chemical fertilisers and pesticides with locally produced organic inputs that are cheaper and thereby generate good returns on ______1______. Organic agriculture also generates income through exports as the demand for organically grown crops is on a _____2___. Studies across countries have shown that organically grown food has more nutritional value than chemical farming, thus providing us with healthy foods. Since organic farming requires more labour input than ____3___ farming, India will find organic farming an attractive______4____. Finally, the produce is pesticide-free and produced in an environmentally ____5____ way.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. proposition.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence concludes a series of positive points about organic farming (cheaper inputs, export income, better nutrition) with: **"India will find organic farming an attractive ___"**. Since organic farming needs more labour, and India has an abundant labour force, this labour-intensive nature becomes an appealing opportunity for India.

• Rule — Idiomatic Collocation: "An attractive proposition" is a standard, fixed collocation in English meaning an appealing idea, plan, or option worth considering — exactly the sense required here (organic farming becomes a worthwhile option for India to pursue).

• The word chosen must also match the uniformly positive, promotional tone of the whole passage, which lists only benefits of organic farming; a word suggesting difficulty would be out of place.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "obstacle" is incorrect because it means a hindrance or barrier, which directly contradicts the positive word "attractive" describing it.

• Option 3: "burden" is incorrect because it means a heavy load/responsibility, again a negative connotation that clashes with "attractive".

• Option 4: "challenge" — this is the option marked as correct in the source answer key, but it fits less well: an "attractive challenge" introduces an incongruous note of difficulty into a sentence that is otherwise entirely positive about organic farming's benefits for India. "An attractive proposition" is the far more natural, idiomatic phrase for describing an appealing course of action, so Option 2 is the better answer.

NOTE

• "Proposition" here means a proposal, plan, or option put forward for consideration — commonly used in the fixed phrase "an attractive/tempting/lucrative proposition".

• Distinguish from "proposal" (a formal suggestion, often for marriage or a plan of action) and "preposition" (a grammatical part of speech) — words often confused with "proposition" due to similar spelling.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Organic agriculture offers a means to substitute costlier agricultural inputs such as HYV seeds, chemical fertilisers and pesticides with locally produced organic inputs that are cheaper and thereby generate good returns on ______1______. Organic agriculture also generates income through exports as the demand for organically grown crops is on a _____2___. Studies across countries have shown that organically grown food has more nutritional value than chemical farming, thus providing us with healthy foods. Since organic farming requires more labour input than ____3___ farming, India will find organic farming an attractive______4____. Finally, the produce is pesticide-free and produced in an environmentally ____5____ way.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. sustainable.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence states that the produce is **"pesticide-free and produced in an environmentally ___ way". Something that is pesticide-free and eco-friendly is best described as environmentally sustainable** — i.e., not causing long-term harm to the environment.

• Rule — Contextual Meaning: The word must complement "pesticide-free" (a positive, eco-friendly quality), continuing the passage's overall positive description of organic farming.

• "Environmentally sustainable" is a widely used fixed phrase describing practices that can be maintained without depleting or damaging natural resources — precisely what organic, pesticide-free farming represents.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "innovative" is incorrect because it means new/original, which does not specifically relate to the environmental friendliness being described alongside "pesticide-free".

• Option 3: "destructive" is incorrect because it means causing great damage, the opposite of the positive quality intended here.

• Option 4: "harmful" is incorrect because it means causing harm, again the opposite of the environmentally positive quality being described.

NOTE

• Common fixed phrase: "environmentally sustainable/friendly", meaning practices that do not damage the environment or exhaust natural resources.

• Related exam vocabulary: sustainability, eco-friendly, biodegradable, renewable — frequently tested in environment-themed cloze passages and reading comprehensions.

question:
Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence.
Neither Janki or I am to receive the award.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. nor.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence uses the correlative conjunction pair "Neither...or", which is grammatically incorrect. The correct pairing is "Neither...nor".

• Rule — Correlative Conjunctions: "Neither" is always paired with "nor", just as "Either" is always paired with "or". These pairs cannot be mixed.

• The underlined word "or" must therefore be replaced with "nor", giving: "Neither Janki nor I am to receive the award."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "either" is incorrect because "either" pairs with "or", not with "neither"; using "either" here would not correct the "neither...or" mismatch.

• Option 2: "no" is incorrect because "no" is not a conjunction and cannot correlate with "neither" to form a grammatically correct structure.

• Option 4: "not" is incorrect because "not" is a simple negator, not a correlative conjunction that pairs with "neither".

NOTE

• Other commonly tested correlative conjunction pairs: both...and, not only...but also, whether...or.

• Subject-Verb Agreement with "neither...nor": the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it — here, "I" is nearer, so the verb is "am" (already correctly used in the sentence).

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution required'.
The film was made in Botswana, whose wildlife parks is larger to those in Kenya.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. are larger than.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined segment "is larger to" contains two separate errors: a subject-verb agreement error and a comparative-degree preposition error.

• Rule 1 — Subject-Verb Agreement: The subject "wildlife parks" is plural, so it must take the plural verb "are", not the singular "is".

• Rule 2 — Comparative Degree: Comparative adjectives ending in "-er" (such as larger, bigger, smaller) must be followed by "than", not "to". ("To" is used with certain comparative words like superior/inferior/senior/junior, not with "-er" comparatives.)

• Correcting both errors gives: "...whose wildlife parks are larger than those in Kenya."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "are large than" is incorrect because "large" is the positive degree, not the comparative degree; a comparison with "than" requires the comparative form "larger".

• Option 3: "No substitution required" is incorrect because the original sentence clearly contains both a subject-verb agreement error and a wrong preposition, as explained above.

• Option 4: "as large than" is incorrect because "as...as" is used for equality (not "as...than"), and mixing "as" with "than" is ungrammatical.

NOTE

• Comparatives with "than": bigger than, smaller than, larger than, better than, worse than.

• Comparatives with "to": superior to, inferior to, senior to, junior to, prior to — these adjectives are of Latin origin and are exceptions to the usual "-er...than" pattern.

question:
Select the most appropriate homophones to fill in the blanks.
It was against her ________ to earn more _________ than that decided by the board of directors.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. principle, profit.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The first blank requires a word meaning a moral rule or personal code of conduct — this is "principle" (noun). It would be "against her principle" to do something she considers wrong.

• The second blank requires a word meaning financial gain — this is "profit", matching the context of earning money "than that decided by the board of directors".

• Rule — Commonly Confused Homophones: "Principle" (a fundamental rule/belief) must not be confused with "Principal" (a) the head of an institution, (b) a leading/main/most important quality (adjective), or (c) an original sum of money (noun, in finance).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "principal; profit" is incorrect because "principal" (head of an institution/chief) does not fit the sense of "a moral rule" required in the first blank.

• Option 3: "principal; prophet" is incorrect for the same reason as Option 2 regarding "principal", and additionally "prophet" (a religious messenger) makes no sense in place of financial gain.

• Option 4: "principle; prophet" is incorrect because although "principle" correctly fills the first blank, "prophet" does not mean financial gain; the required word is "profit".

NOTE

• Principle vs Principal: Principle = a rule/law/belief (noun only); Principal = head of a school/college (noun) OR main/most important (adjective) OR the original amount of a loan/investment (noun, finance).

• Profit vs Prophet: Profit = financial gain; Prophet = a person who speaks on behalf of God/predicts the future — a commonly tested homophone pair in SSC exams.

question:
Select the most appropriate homophones to fill in the blanks.
I _________ that he has been promoted to the post of _____ officer.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. heard; sealing.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The first blank requires the past tense of "hear" (to perceive with the ears), which is "heard". "Herd" (a group of animals) does not fit the sentence's meaning.

• The second blank requires a word that can describe a type of "officer". "Sealing officer" refers to an official designation (an officer responsible for sealing/verification duties), whereas "ceiling" (the upper interior surface of a room, or an upper limit) cannot sensibly describe a post/officer designation here.

• Rule — Commonly Confused Homophones: "Heard" (past tense of "hear") must not be confused with "Herd" (a group of animals); "Sealing" (the act of closing/fixing a seal, from the verb "seal") must not be confused with "Ceiling" (the top interior surface of a room, or a maximum limit).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "herd; sealing" is incorrect because "herd" (a group of animals) makes no sense as the verb needed in the first blank; the sentence needs "heard" (past tense of hear).

• Option 3: "herd; ceiling" is incorrect for both blanks — "herd" does not fit the first blank, and "ceiling" does not fit as a job designation in the second.

• Option 4: "heard; ceiling" is incorrect because, while "heard" correctly fills the first blank, "ceiling" cannot describe a type of officer/post; "sealing" is required.

NOTE

• Heard vs Herd: Heard = past tense/participle of "hear"; Herd = a group of cattle or other animals.

• Sealing vs Ceiling: Sealing = the act of closing something tightly or fixing an official seal on it (from the verb "seal"); Ceiling = the upper interior surface of a room, or figuratively, an upper limit (e.g., "price ceiling").

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
To throw dust in one's eyes
option_1: To talk in an abusive language
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. To mislead someone by tricks.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "To throw dust in someone's eyes" means to deliberately deceive or mislead someone by hiding the truth or using clever tricks. (किसी को धोखा देना / गुमराह करना)
◦ Example: The salesman threw dust in the customer's eyes by hiding the product's real defects.

• The idiom draws on the literal image of throwing dust into someone's eyes to temporarily blind or confuse them so they cannot see clearly — figuratively, it means clouding someone's judgment with deception.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: To talk in an abusive language describes the idiom "to talk trash" or "to use foul language", not this idiom.

• Option 3: To make someone blind forever is incorrect because the idiom is figurative, referring to temporary deception, not literal or permanent blindness.

• Option 4: To hit someone with stone describes a completely different, literal act unrelated to this idiom's meaning of deception.

NOTE

• Other idioms of deception commonly tested by SSC: "To pull the wool over someone's eyes" (to deceive someone), "To take someone for a ride" (to cheat/fool someone), and "To lead someone up the garden path" (to mislead someone).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Queer
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Ordinary.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Queer" means strange, odd, or unusual (अजीब / विचित्र). Its antonym must mean the opposite — something normal or usual.

• "Ordinary" means normal, usual, not different or special in any way (सामान्य), which is the direct opposite of "strange/odd".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Doubtful" means uncertain or unsure, which is not an antonym of "queer"; it relates to a different concept altogether.

• Option 2: "Fantastic" means excellent or extraordinary, which is actually closer in meaning to "queer" (unusual) than opposite to it.

• Option 3: "Eccentric" means unconventional or odd in behaviour, which is a near-synonym of "queer", not its antonym.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "queer": odd, bizarre, peculiar, strange, weird.

• Other antonyms of "queer": normal, usual, conventional, common.

question: Select the correctly spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Quintessential.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Quintessential" — meaning representing the most perfect or typical example of a quality or class.

• Spelling key: QUINT + ESS + ENTIAL. Note the double "s" in the middle syllable "-ess-", and the ending "-ential" (not "-intial" or a swapped vowel). The word derives from "quintessence", itself from the Latin quinta essentia ("fifth essence").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Quintessintial" is incorrect; the vowel after "ess" should be "e" (as in "essential"), not "i".

• Option 3: "Quintesential" is incorrect; the double "s" in "-ess-" has been wrongly reduced to a single "s".

• Option 4: "Quientessential" is incorrect; the letters "u" and "i" after "Q" have been wrongly reversed — it should be "Quint-", not "Quient-".

NOTE

• Related word: quintessence (the most perfect example or purest essence of something).

• Other commonly misspelt "-ential/-ancial" ending words tested by SSC: influential, confidential, essential, financial, residential.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank and complete the sentence.
You just wait in the lobby. I will be back after _________.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. a quick shower.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The words "quick" and "fast" are near-synonyms but are used with different collocations. "Quick" describes something that takes a short amount of time, while "fast" describes something that moves at a high speed.

• Rule — Collocation: Activities that are brief in duration (not necessarily high-speed) collocate with "quick" — e.g., a quick shower, a quick meal, a quick glance, a quick nap. "Fast" collocates with things that move rapidly — e.g., a fast car, a fast runner.

• Since a "shower" is an activity measured by how briefly it is completed (not by speed of movement), "a quick shower" is the natural, idiomatic collocation.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "a fast meal" is incorrect collocation; a brief meal is described as "a quick meal", not "a fast meal" (though "fast food" is a distinct fixed term with a different meaning — ready-made, quickly served food).

• Option 3: "a fast shower" is incorrect for the same reason — a shower is described by duration ("quick"), not speed ("fast").

• Option 4: "a quick food" is incorrect because "food" is an uncountable/general noun and does not idiomatically follow "a quick"; "a quick meal" would be correct, but "a quick food" is not natural English.

NOTE

• Commonly tested "quick" collocations: a quick look, a quick decision, a quick word, a quick shower, a quick nap.

• Commonly tested "fast" collocations: a fast car, a fast train, a fast worker, fast food (a fixed compound noun, not "quick food").

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Anxiety
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Distress.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Anxiety" means a feeling of worry, nervousness, or unease about something with an uncertain outcome (चिंता / व्याकुलता).

• "Distress" means extreme anxiety, sorrow, or pain (पीड़ा / संकट) — it shares the core sense of mental unease/suffering with "anxiety", making it the closest synonym among the options.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Serenity" means calmness and peacefulness, which is the opposite of anxiety, not a synonym.

• Option 3: "Dilemma" means a situation requiring a difficult choice between two options; it does not mean a feeling of worry, so it is not a true synonym.

• Option 4: "Ease" means comfort or freedom from difficulty, which is again opposite in meaning to anxiety.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "anxiety": worry, unease, apprehension, nervousness, angst.

• Antonyms of "anxiety": calm, composure, serenity, ease, tranquillity.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the word 'Contaminate' from the given sentence.
Crews were requested to purify the system since a brain-eating amoeba was discovered in the drinking water.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. purify.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Contaminate" means to make something impure or dirty by adding a polluting or harmful substance (दूषित करना).

• "Purify" means to make something clean by removing dirty, harmful, or unwanted substances (शुद्ध करना) — this is the direct opposite of "contaminate", making it the correct antonym found within the sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "requested" simply means "asked for" and has no meaning-based connection to "contaminate" or its opposite.

• Option 2: "discovered" means "found out" and is unrelated in meaning to "contaminate"/"purify".

• Option 4: "system" is merely a noun referring to the water system in the sentence; it carries no opposite meaning to "contaminate".

NOTE

• Other antonyms of "contaminate": cleanse, disinfect, decontaminate, sanitise.

• Other synonyms of "contaminate": pollute, taint, infect, corrupt, adulterate.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The guard did not want anything bad to happen, so he ordered the group to step back to avoid anything _________.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. terrible.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence begins by stating that the guard "did not want anything bad to happen", and then explains the reason he ordered the group to step back: to avoid anything ___. The blank must therefore restate/match the idea of "anything bad".

• Rule — Contextual Consistency: The correct option must be consistent in meaning with an earlier part of the same sentence. Since "bad" was already used, the blank needs a near-synonym of "bad" that fits naturally — "terrible" (extremely bad, causing fear or harm) fits this sense perfectly.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "customary" means usual/traditional, which does not connect logically to wanting to avoid something after fearing something "bad".

• Option 3: "habitual" means done regularly as a habit; it does not carry the negative sense required to match "anything bad".

• Option 4: "diplomatic" means tactful in dealing with people, which is unrelated to the sentence's context of danger or harm.

NOTE

• Words expressing something undesirable/dangerous, often tested in similar fill-in-the-blank contexts: terrible, dreadful, disastrous, unfortunate, harmful.

• Always look for a keyword earlier in the sentence (here, "bad") that hints at the required meaning of the blank.

question:
Rectify the sentence by selecting the correct spelling from the options.
Psycology developed as a significant discipline of study in the twentieth century.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Psychology.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Psychology" — the scientific study of the human mind and behaviour.

• Spelling key: PSY + CHO + LOGY. Note the silent "p" at the start, followed by "sy", then "cho" (not "cy" or "ci"), and the standard "-logy" ending used for fields of study.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Pscycology" is incorrect; it wrongly inserts a "c" before "y" as "pscy-" instead of the correct "psy-".

• Option 3: "Pcychology" is incorrect; the letters "s" and "c" after "p" have been wrongly reversed — it should be "psy-", not "pcy-".

• Option 4: "Pscichology" is incorrect; it wrongly spells the middle syllable as "-ci-" instead of the correct "-cho-".

NOTE

• Related words with the same "psy-" root (from Greek "psyche", meaning mind/soul): psychiatry, psychologist, psychic, psychosomatic.

• Other "-logy" ending words frequently tested for spelling: biology, technology, sociology, chronology.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom in the given sentence.
Every piece of furniture in her house is in apple-pie order.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Very neatly arranged.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "in apple-pie order" means arranged very neatly and tidily; in perfect order (एकदम व्यवस्थित / करीने से रखा हुआ).
◦ Example: Before the guests arrived, she made sure the entire house was in apple-pie order.

• The phrase likely originates from the neat, orderly layers in which apple slices are traditionally arranged inside a pie, symbolising careful, systematic arrangement.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Painted in light colours" describes a literal visual/colour quality, which has nothing to do with this idiom's meaning of tidiness.

• Option 3: "Very delicately arranged" is incorrect because the idiom emphasises neatness/orderliness, not delicacy or fragility of arrangement.

• Option 4: "Kept in a disorganised way" is the opposite of the idiom's actual meaning; "apple-pie order" specifically denotes a high degree of tidiness.

NOTE

• Other idioms of neatness/order commonly tested by SSC: "Spick and span" (very clean and tidy), "Shipshape" (in good order), and "Neat as a pin" (extremely tidy).

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
He has recovered now and is feeling too strong to walk.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. strong enough to walk.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined segment "too strong to walk" is logically flawed: the structure "too + adjective + to + verb" means the quality is present in such excess that the action becomes impossible — so "too strong to walk" would illogically mean he is SO strong that he CANNOT walk.

• Rule — "Too...to" vs "Enough...to": "Too + adjective + to + verb" expresses a negative result (excess prevents the action), while "Adjective + enough + to + verb" expresses a positive result (sufficient quality enables the action).

• Since the sentence means the person has recovered and is now capable of walking, the correct structure is "strong enough to walk" — sufficiently strong to be able to walk.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "too weak to walk" is incorrect because it means he is unable to walk due to weakness, which contradicts the idea that he "has recovered".

• Option 2: "weak enough to walk" is incorrect and illogical; being "weak enough" would not enable walking — "enough" should follow a positive/enabling quality like "strong", not "weak".

• Option 3: "strong to walk" is incorrect because it is grammatically incomplete; the "enough" is missing, without which "strong to walk" makes no proper structural sense.

NOTE

• "Too" structure: too + adjective + to + verb → negative/impossible result (e.g., too tired to run).

• "Enough" structure: adjective + enough + to + verb → positive/possible result (e.g., fast enough to win) — note "enough" comes AFTER the adjective, unlike "too" which comes BEFORE it.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Peter was the last to know that she had been cheating of him.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. cheating on him.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrasal verb meaning to be unfaithful to a partner in a relationship is "to cheat on someone", which always takes the preposition "on".

• Rule — Fixed Preposition with Phrasal Verbs: Many verbs combine with a specific, fixed preposition to form an idiomatic phrasal verb, and this preposition cannot be substituted with another one of similar general meaning. "Cheat", in the sense of being unfaithful, is fixed with "on".

• The underlined "cheating of him" wrongly uses "of" instead of the required "on", so it must be corrected to "cheating on him".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "cheating up him" is incorrect; "up" is not the preposition used with "cheat" in this sense, and this phrasing is not standard English.

• Option 2: "cheating in him" is incorrect; "in" does not form part of this fixed phrasal verb.

• Option 3: "cheat of him" is incorrect; besides the wrong preposition "of", the base form "cheat" (instead of "cheating") also breaks the required continuous tense structure ("had been cheating").

NOTE

• Other verbs with fixed prepositions frequently tested by SSC: rely on, depend on, insist on, believe in, differ from, deal with.

• "Cheat someone (out) of something" (a different sense, meaning to swindle someone of money/property) uses "of" — but that is a distinct meaning from "being unfaithful", which uses "on".

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word.
I left the job because of a hostile working environment.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Friendly.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Hostile" means unfriendly, antagonistic, or opposed (शत्रुतापूर्ण / प्रतिकूल).

• "Friendly" means kind, warm, and pleasant towards others (मैत्रीपूर्ण), which is the direct opposite of "hostile", making it the correct antonym.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Morose" means sullen or gloomy in mood, which is a near-synonym of an unpleasant disposition, not an antonym of "hostile".

• Option 3: "Rustic" means relating to the countryside or simple/rural in character; it is unrelated in meaning to "hostile" or its opposite.

• Option 4: "Violent" means using or involving physical force, which is actually related in meaning to "hostile" (aggressive), not its opposite.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "hostile": antagonistic, unfriendly, adversarial, belligerent.

• Other antonyms of "hostile": amicable, cordial, welcoming, hospitable.
